newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech spymaster quits in row before key elections.
newsitem.headline: Czech spymaster quits in row before key elections.

text.p: The acting director of the Czech state intelligence agency BIS resigned on Monday amid allegations it spied on a cabinet minister, raising tensions within the ruling coalition just days before key elections.

Government spokesman Ivo Strejcek told Reuters that Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus had accepted the resignation of Stanislav Devaty, which followed allegations the BIS had spied on Deputy Prime Minister Josef Lux and then tried to cover up their actions.

Devaty, a controversial protege of Klaus, quit four days before voting begins in Senate elections, the first test of the centre-right coalition government since it lost its lower house majority six months ago.

The scandal, the second such row in the past two years, provoked public squabbling between the Christian Democrats, a junior coalition partner led by Lux, and Klaus, who leads the conservative Civic Democratic Party (ODS).
Lux, who is also agriculture minister, triggered the row last Friday by alleging that the BIS had spied on him three years ago and then covered up their action.
"I am not troubled by the fact that I was shadowed. What is disturbing about it is the fact that it was hidden from the inspection authorities," he said on Czech Television on Sunday.
The row has several ingredients of a Cold War spy novel: shadowing, bugging and missing pages from intelligence reports.
According to Czech newspapers, the BIS planted an agent codenamed "Pramen" ("Source") in the Agriculture Ministry.

But the BIS is supposed to have called off the operation because of its political nature. Two pages on the Lux operation were removed from a BIS report to a parliamentary commission and the cabinet to keep it secret, newspapers reported.
Klaus, whose ODS heads the coalition, reacted amgrily Lux's allegations, saying: "I strongly reject the term that he "was followed'."
The premier inked the timing of the spying revelations to the Senate elections, the first round of which will be held on Friday and Saturday.
It was not by chance that "somebody pulled this out a week before an election", he said. Lux said he had only now been tipped off about the operation three years ago.

The Senate has few powers compared with the lower chamber, where the coalition narrowly lost its majority in June. But analysts say the Senate elections, which have a second round run-off on November 22-23, are crucial to Klaus's future.
If his ODS does well, he may be tempted to provoke early lower house elections in an attempt to regain his majority. If he does badly, his job may be on the line.
Devaty, who has never been confirmed as BIS director even though he has been in the job for several years, is a member of the ODS but suspended his membership when he became spymaster.
Klaus said at the weekend the spying had not been aimed at Lux but at one of his advisers, banker Antonin Moravec.

Moravec was director of Kreditni a Prumyslova Banka, which collapsed in a fraud scandal in 1993. Moravec, a Christian Democrat election organiser, was also involved with an former communist general in plans to redevelop part of a disused Soviet airbase north of Prague.
A spokesman for President Vaclav Havel described Devaty's resignation as a reasonable step. The cabinet had been due to discuss Devaty's future on Wednesday.

Coalition bickering over spy charges is nothing new. Early last year the leader of the other junior coalition partner, Deputy Prime Minister Jan Kalvoda, accused the BIS of spying on his Civic Democratic Alliance (ODA).
Lux chimed in at the time that the Christian Democrats had also been a target of BIS activity. Those allegations were never substantiated and Devaty resisted pressure to quit.
